prompt: Match each input of a sample-size calculation to what it is.

pairs.right: the chance of a false alarm
the chance of detecting a real effect

right_distractors: the length of the test in days

prompt: Where should the minimum detectable effect come from?

choices.text: The effect the team expects to see
choices.why: A test sized for an optimistic expectation is too small for a realistic effect.

choices.text: The smallest effect that would pay for the change
choices.why: Right. It is a business judgement.

choices.text: Whatever effect fits the traffic available this month, so the test can finish on schedule
choices.why: That decides the question by the calendar; the honest move is to say the test can only rule out large effects.

choices.text: The p-value of the last test
choices.why: A p-value is not an effect size.

prompt: A test is planned with 80% power. What does that promise?

choices.text: If the true lift equals the MDE, a significant result 80% of the time
choices.why: Right. And less often for smaller real effects.

choices.text: An 80% chance the treatment is better
choices.why: Power says nothing about whether the treatment is better.

choices.text: That 80% of visitors are included
choices.why: That is the traffic share, a different number.

choices.text: A false alarm in one test of five
choices.why: False alarms are α, 5%.

prompt: With α = 5% and power = 80%, how do the two risks of a test compare?

choices.text: They are equal
choices.why: β is 20% and α is 5%.

choices.text: A false alarm is four times as likely as a miss
choices.why: The other way round.

choices.text: The two add up to 100%
choices.why: They are separate risks under different truths.

choices.text: The risk of missing a real effect is four times the risk of a false alarm
choices.why: Right: 20% against 5%.

prompt: What z-value does a two-sided 5% significance level use, to two decimal places?
By the textbook formula, how many visitors does each group of Panela's test need?
In the sample-size formula, what is in the denominator, and how?

choices.text: The baseline rate, once
choices.why: The baseline sits in the numerator, inside the spread of a proportion.

choices.text: The number of days the test will run, which converts visitors into time
choices.why: Days come afterwards, from the traffic.

choices.text: The MDE, squared
choices.why: Right. That square is the lesson's main fact.

choices.text: The power, squared
choices.why: Power enters through its z-value in the numerator.

prompt: The formula gives 18,739 and statsmodels 18,719. Which should the plan use?

choices.text: The average, 18,729
choices.why: Averaging two approximations adds nothing; the convention is simpler.

choices.text: The larger, rounded up
choices.why: Right. It is a planning number.

choices.text: statsmodels', since a library is always more accurate than a formula typed by hand
choices.why: Both are approximations; neither is exact.

choices.text: Neither: rerun until they agree
choices.why: They are different approximations and will not.

prompt: A test needs 20,000 visitors per group to detect a 1-point lift. About how many would it need for a 0.5-point lift?
A shop with 300 visitors a day wants to test a new button colour expected to lift conversion by 2% relative. What is the best advice?

choices.text: Test a bolder change
choices.why: Right. Small sites need big effects to see anything.

choices.text: Run it for a month and see
choices.why: A month is far too short for an effect that small; the result will almost surely be inconclusive.

choices.text: Lower α to 20% so it finishes quickly
choices.why: That buys speed with false alarms.

choices.text: Count page views instead of visitors to get a larger sample from the same traffic
choices.why: More rows that depend on each other are not more information.

prompt: On a 4.2% baseline, a lift of 0.6 points is about what relative lift?

choices.why: That confuses points with per cent.
That is the treatment's rate, not the lift.
Off by a factor of four.

prompt: An underpowered test happens to come out significant. What should a reader suspect?

choices.text: Nothing; significant is significant
choices.why: Significance says the effect is not zero, not that its size is right.

choices.text: The effect is probably smaller than zero
choices.why: The sign is usually right; the size is the problem.

choices.text: The estimated effect is probably too large
choices.why: Right. Only the lucky high draws cross the line in a small test.

choices.text: The power must have been miscalculated
choices.why: It can be right and still produce this; it is a property of small tests.

prompt: Two groups of 18,739 visitors at 2,400 visitors a day: how many days of traffic, rounded up?
Why round a test's 16 days up to 21?

choices.text: Statistics needs a multiple of seven
choices.why: The formula does not care; the calendar does.

choices.text: Whole weeks weigh every weekday equally
choices.why: Right. Visitors of different weekdays may behave differently.

choices.text: For extra power, as a safety margin in case the baseline turns out lower than planned
choices.why: The power gain is a side effect, not the reason.

choices.text: Tests must last three weeks
choices.why: The length depends on traffic and sample; three weeks is this test's.

prompt: The same test with only 20% of the traffic: how many days, rounded up?
A large site reaches its sample in three days. Why still run for a full week?

choices.text: Three days hold no weekend and only three weekdays
choices.why: Right. The result would describe part of the week.

choices.text: The servers need time to warm up
choices.why: Nothing technical requires it.

choices.text: Power drops after three days
choices.why: Power rises with visitors.

choices.text: Statistics forbids tests shorter than a week, since the formula assumes seven days of data
choices.why: The formula assumes nothing about days.

items: choose baseline, MDE, α and power
